questions.q: A student states: "Primary Health Care is only about treating minor illnesses like cold and fever." Is this statement correct? Explain why or why not using the NCERT definition.
questions.a: The statement is incorrect. NCERT defines Primary Health Care as "the first level of contact between individuals with the health care system" – it includes preventive, promotive, and therapeutic care, not just curative treatment of minor ailments. PHC encompasses immunisation, maternal-child health, health education, sanitation, and disease surveillance. A wrong answer reveals the student equates "primary" with "simple treatment" rather than "first contact point for comprehensive care."

questions.q: A pregnant woman in a remote village receives iron-folic acid tablets and antenatal check-ups from an ANM at the Sub-Centre. At 36 weeks, she develops severe anaemia (Hb 7 g/dL) and is sent to the Community Health Centre (CHC) for IV iron therapy. Classify the care received at Sub-Centre and CHC into primary/secondary/tertiary levels and justify each classification.
questions.a: Sub-Centre care = Primary (first contact, preventive/promotive antenatal care by ANM). CHC care = Secondary (referral from primary, specialised treatment – IV iron requires medical officer/specialist and facility infrastructure not available at Sub-Centre). A wrong answer (e.g., calling CHC "tertiary") reveals confusion between "specialised" (secondary) and "super-specialised/intensive" (tertiary) – CHCs lack ICU, ventilators, and super-specialists that define tertiary care.

questions.q: A 45-year-old farmer suffers a heart attack. His family rushes him directly to a medical college hospital 80 km away, bypassing the PHC and district hospital. He dies en route. Using the three-level framework, analyse TWO system failures illustrated by this scenario.
questions.a: Failure 1: Bypassing primary care – PHC could have given aspirin, oxygen, and arranged ambulance with ECG monitoring during transfer (the "golden hour" principle). Failure 2: Absence of functional referral linkage – no established protocol for emergency referral from PHC → CHC → tertiary with pre-notification. A wrong answer focusing only on "distance" or "poverty" misses the structural failure: the system design assumes stepwise referral, but communities lack trust/awareness of primary level emergency capacity.

questions.q: Compare and contrast the gatekeeping function of Primary Health Care in India's public system versus a hypothetical system where patients can directly access tertiary hospitals without referral. Use the concepts of resource allocation, equity, and clinical appropriateness.
questions.a: With gatekeeping: Resources (specialists, MRI, ICU beds) concentrate on complex cases; equity improves as rural poor access first-contact care locally; clinical appropriateness ensures simple conditions don't block super-specialised slots. Without gatekeeping: Tertiary hospitals overload with minor ailments (studies show 60-70% OPD cases at AIIMS are primary-care treatable); rural patients incur catastrophic travel/opportunity costs; specialists spend time on UTIs instead of transplants. A weak answer lists only "crowding" without linking to equity or clinical triage logic.

questions.q: "India should convert all Primary Health Centres into mini-hospitals with X-ray, lab, and specialist doctors to reduce referral burden." Evaluate this proposal against the Alma-Ata principles of Primary Health Care and the NCERT definition of three-tier care.
questions.a: The proposal violates Alma-Ata's core principle: PHC must be "universally accessible, affordable, and community-participatory" – adding high-tech diagnostics shifts focus from preventive/promotive to curative, escalates costs, and creates "mini-hospitals" that drain resources from community outreach. NCERT's three-tier model explicitly defines secondary care as the level for "specialised hospital like district hospitals" – upgrading PHCs blurs the referral boundary, causing duplication (two levels doing same work) and leaving tertiary centres without a filtered referral stream. A poor answer supports the proposal citing "better facilities" without addressing system-level consequences.

questions.q: Design a flowchart for a 10-year-old child in a tribal village who develops fever → rash → joint pain → suspected rheumatic heart disease. Show the referral pathway across all three levels, specifying at each level: (a) cadre of provider, (b) key diagnostic/therapeutic action, (c) referral trigger to next level.
questions.a: Level 1 (Primary – Sub-Centre/PHC): Provider = ANM/MPW/MO; Action = Clinical diagnosis (Jones criteria), throat swab, inj. penicillin prophylaxis; Trigger = Heart murmur detected / echo needed. Level 2 (Secondary – CHC/District Hospital): Provider = Paediatrician/Physician; Action = Echo confirmation, ASD/VSD ruling out, long-acting penicillin, heart failure management; Trigger = Valve damage needing surgery / complex arrhythmia. Level 3 (Tertiary – Medical College): Provider = Paediatric Cardiologist/CTVS; Action = Valve repair/replacement, catheter intervention, lifelong anticoagulation management. A poor answer lists only institutions without specifying cadres, actions, or triggers – showing memorisation without clinical reasoning.
